introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 3 (0760), Paper 3 - Africa and World History, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2022. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections (Section A: Africa, 1800-1945; Section B: Africa, 1945 to the present; Section C: World Revolutions and Diplomacy, 1700-1919; Section D: World, 1919 to the present date). All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
enonce_intro_markdown: **SECTION D: WORLD, 1919 TO THE PRESENT DATE**
incertitudes: Règle de choix : le sujet impose « answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections ». `regles_choix` porte une règle « 1 sur 3 » par section (A, B, C, D), ce qui correspond exactement à la consigne imprimée ; la consigne complète est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`.

Points : chaque question porte 25 marks imprimés (« All questions carry equal marks »), soit 100 points pour les quatre questions à traiter. Aucun écart de points constaté ; `points` vaut 25 pour l'exercice et pour l'unique question de chaque fichier.

Sujet scanné de deux pages (page de garde et questions 1 à 12) ; filigranes gcerevision ignorés. Le texte de la page 2 transparaît en miroir sur la page de garde (verso mal opacifié) et quelques espaces sont manquants à l'impression (question 8 : « between1871and1890 », rétabli en « between 1871 and 1890 ») ; aucune question coupée ni illisible, aucune figure ni carte dans le sujet.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées au niveau Advanced Level (introduction, développement, conclusion argumentée). Aucune citation n'est inventée et les chiffres sont limités à des repères datés de l'historiographie courante (dates, traités) ; à relire par un historien avant mise en vente.

Question 4 : l'énoncé imprimé date le déclenchement de la révolte Mau Mau de 1951. L'historiographie situe la montée de la violence en 1950-52 (mouvement interdit en août 1950, état d'urgence proclamé le 20 octobre 1952) ; le sujet est recopié tel quel et le corrigé précise la chronologie sans corriger l'énoncé.

Question 5 : l'Afrique équatoriale française regroupe le Gabon, le Moyen-Congo, l'Oubangui-Chari et le Tchad ; le Cameroun, ancien mandat puis tutelle, n'en faisait pas partie. Les interventions militaires françaises (Gabon 1964, Tchad à partir de la fin des années 1960, Centrafrique 1979) et le rôle du réseau Foccart sont cités selon l'historiographie courante, sans chiffres.

Question 7 : le sujet emploie « romanisation » au sens de la promotion du catholicisme romain par Jacques II ; les dates de 1688 sont données en style ancien (naissance du prince le 10 juin, acquittement des sept évêques et invitation à Guillaume le 30 juin, débarquement à Torbay le 5 novembre).

Question 9 : le montant des réparations (132 milliards de marks-or, fixé en 1921) et les pertes territoriales sont cités de mémoire historique établie ; aucune statistique de population n'est avancée.

Question 11 : la Banque mondiale et le FMI sont des institutions spécialisées de l'ONU ; l'UNICEF (fonds et non institution spécialisée) n'est volontairement pas traité. Les dates (variole déclarée éradiquée en 1980, Alma-Ata 1978, convention 182 de l'OIT en 1999, Codex Alimentarius 1963, retrait des États-Unis de l'UNESCO en 1984-85) sont citées selon l'historiographie courante.

Question 12 : le sujet vise la rupture sino-soviétique après la mort de Staline (1953). Les dates (discours de Khrouchtchev en février 1956, rupture de l'accord nucléaire en 1959, retrait des conseillers en 1960, congrès de Bucarest en juin 1960, guerre sino-indienne 1962, incidents de l'Oussouri en mars 1969) sont données selon l'historiographie courante ; aucun chiffre n'est avancé.

Thèmes : les noms sont qualifiés pour éviter les collisions avec les Tags de l'Histoire francophone (`sino-soviet split`, `afrikaner nationalism`, `mau mau revolt in kenya`...) ; plusieurs sont réutilisés des sujets History 2020-2021 (`scramble for africa`, `apartheid in south africa`, `cold war`, `indirect rule in colonial africa`) ; à revérifier à l'ingestion avec `find_tag_variant`.

questions.enonce_markdown:
To what do you attribute the rift between China and USSR after 1953?

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** In 1950 the People's Republic of China, which had come to power in 1949 under Mao Zedong, and the Soviet Union signed a Treaty of Friendship, Alliance and Mutual Assistance, and in the early 1950s the two communist powers seemed to form a united bloc. After the death of Stalin in March 1953, however, relations deteriorated, with open disagreement by 1960 and armed border clashes in 1969 (on the Ussuri River). The split resulted from a combination of ideological differences, disputes about leadership of world communism, national interests, border and territorial questions, and the personalities of their leaders.

**1. Ideological disagreements.**
- *De-Stalinisation.* In February 1956, at the 20th Congress of the Soviet Communist Party, Nikita Khrushchev denounced Stalin's crimes and the "cult of personality". Mao regarded Stalin as a great Marxist leader and feared that the attack would weaken communism and also reflect on his own position as a leader with a personality cult.
- *Peaceful coexistence.* Khrushchev argued that war with capitalism was not inevitable and that communism could win through peaceful competition. Mao thought that this was a betrayal of revolutionary principles and that the West should be confronted, and the Chinese accused the Soviets of "revisionism", while the Soviets accused the Chinese of "dogmatism" and "adventurism".
- *Different roads to communism.* China's Great Leap Forward (1958) and the communes, an attempt to build communism quickly by mass mobilisation, were criticised by the Soviets as unrealistic, while Mao regarded the Soviet model as too cautious and bureaucratic.

**2. Rivalry for leadership of the communist world.** Mao, who had led a successful peasant revolution on his own, saw himself as a senior theorist of Marxism after Stalin's death and resented the Soviet claim to leadership. China also competed with the USSR for influence among Asian, African and Latin American communist movements and newly independent states.

**3. National interests and practical disputes.**
- *Nuclear weapons.* The USSR had at first helped China's nuclear programme, but in 1959 it ended the agreement to provide a sample bomb and technical help, since Khrushchev wished to avoid the spread of nuclear weapons and was seeking an improvement in relations with the USA (Camp David, 1959). China felt let down and then developed its own bomb, which it tested in 1964.
- *Taiwan and the Offshore Islands.* In 1958 China shelled the Quemoy islands, and the USSR was reluctant to risk war with the USA to support it.
- *Soviet aid and advisers.* China resented Soviet attitudes and the terms of loans, and in 1960 the USSR withdrew its technical advisers from China, which was a serious blow to Chinese industry.
- *India.* The USSR's friendly relations with India and its neutral attitude in the Sino-Indian border war of 1962 angered China.
- *The Cuban Missile Crisis (1962).* Mao accused Khrushchev of recklessness in putting missiles in Cuba and then of weakness in withdrawing them; the signing of the Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty in 1963 with the USA and Britain was also condemned by China.

**4. Border and territorial disputes.** China claimed that large areas of territory in the north and north-west had been taken by Tsarist Russia through the "unequal treaties" of the nineteenth century (such as Aigun in 1858 and Peking in 1860). Disagreements on the border, which was long, led to growing tension and clashes in March 1969 on the Ussuri River near Zhenbao (Damansky) Island.

**5. Personalities.** The personal dislike and mistrust between Mao and Khrushchev (for example after Khrushchev's visit to Beijing in 1958, when a Soviet proposal for joint naval facilities offended Mao) also made compromise harder.

**6. Consequences.** The open split was visible by 1960, the year of the quarrels at the Romanian Communist Party Congress in Bucharest and the withdrawal of Soviet experts. It divided the communist world, weakened the unity of the bloc in the Cold War, and eventually led China to move closer to the USA in the early 1970s (Nixon's visit in 1972).

**Conclusion.** The rift after 1953 cannot be attributed to a single cause. The immediate trigger was de-Stalinisation and the Soviet policy of peaceful coexistence, which Mao rejected on ideological grounds, but it deepened because of rivalry for leadership of communism, differences over nuclear weapons and aid, border disputes, and the personal relations of Mao and Khrushchev. Ideology and national interest worked together.
